reader.summary: DR Congo's Ebola outbreak worsened sharply during this window. The disease spread to an eighth province, the total caseload surpassed 6,000, and confirmed cases emerged in at least four neighboring countries. Nigeria reported its first case, which matched the DR Congo strain, and Kenya saw its cases climb to eight. In response, the WHO and partners launched a clinical trial for a three-dose Ebola vaccine in the country. The human toll deepened: hundreds of children were orphaned, prompting emergency nurseries, and grieving families reported a growing mental health burden. Meanwhile, former President Joseph Kabila formally aligned himself with the M23 rebellion, a move Belgium called 'incomprehensible and unacceptable.' Kinshasa tightened its diplomatic posture by barring presidential-office staff from speaking with the Belgian embassy. A cadre of President Tshisekedi's party was arrested for calling to distribute weapons to the public. On the economic front, a US-backed mining company entered final negotiations with Glencore. The national census in Kinshasa continued to face logistical and political obstacles, with officials describing the setbacks as a response to population demands.

crystal.summary: The coming week in DR Congo will be defined by the Ebola outbreak's relentless expansion beyond the country's borders. A fifth neighboring state will confirm a case tied to the Congolese strain, and the fresh vaccine trial will generate its first round of public commentary. In Kinshasa, the political fallout from the ruling party cadre's call to arm the public against Westerners will widen into a second detention or censure, deepening the internal fracture. On the economic front, the Glencore minerals deal will close, giving the government a rare positive headline. The standoff with Brussels will hold steady as both sides digest the Kabila-M23 alliance without a new dramatic gesture. The census in Kinshasa will recede from the front pages. Overall, the epidemic will dominate the narrative, the political infighting will sharpen, and the mining deal will provide a brief counterpoint of normalcy.

display.eli5:
Right now in DR Congo, two big things are happening at the same time. The Ebola virus is spreading fast — it is already in eight provinces and four other countries, and thousands of people are sick. At the same time, the politicians in Kinshasa are fighting each other: one of the president's own party members got arrested for saying the country should hand out guns to fight Westerners.

The reason things are getting worse is that the virus keeps finding new routes out of the eastern provinces, and the political split gives the government fewer people it can trust to manage the crisis. The new vaccine trial just started, so there is hope, but it is too early to tell if it works.

Next week, the Ebola story will probably get even bigger — another country might confirm a case, and the vaccine trial will start making news. The political fight will also get louder, with probably another arrest or public scolding inside the president's party.

The big surprise would be if the weird case in Nigeria — a Swiss person who never even visited DR Congo but still got Ebola — makes a European country shut its borders to the eastern provinces. That would turn a local epidemic into a global headline overnight.

Former President Joseph Kabila formally joined the AFC/M23 rebel coalition in eastern Congo; Kinshasa denounced the move as a prelude to a 'generalized attack' and warned that Kabila's own political family was fracturing over it. The development raised fresh fears that ongoing peace efforts in the east could unravel. The Ebola outbreak also accelerated sharply. The virus spread to an eighth province bordering Central Africa, the UN warned the epidemic was growing 'exponentially,' and the Africa CDC revealed over $700 million in pledged response funds remained unaccounted for. Fearing contagion, mothers in affected areas skipped vital maternal and pediatric care, prompting authorities to launch an improved vaccination drive in Beni. Diplomatically, tensions flared with Brussels after Belgian police searched the homes of President Tshisekedi's relatives; the DRC presidency then restricted its staff's contact with the Belgian embassy.
